subsection: 1. Coastal processes, patterns and associated landforms

notes.b: Waves take their energy from the wind, and the water itself stays in place as the wave passes. Knowing how a wave forms and breaks explains everything the sea later does to the coast.
points: Wind blowing over the sea surface transfers energy to the water, raising waves.
Wave size depends on wind speed, the length of time the wind blows, and fetch.
Fetch is the distance of open water over which the wind blows; a longer fetch allows bigger waves because the wind has more distance in which to pass energy to the water.
Water particles move in circles as a wave passes, so it is the energy that travels, not the water; the water does not travel forward until the wave breaks.
A wave's crest is its highest point and its trough the lowest; wave height is the vertical distance between them, and wavelength is the distance between successive crests.
A wave breaks in shallow water: friction with the sea bed slows its base while the crest keeps moving, so the crest topples forward.
Swash is the water rushing up the beach after a wave breaks, carrying sand and shingle with it.
Backwash is the water draining back down the beach under gravity, so it can pull material back down with it, which is why the swash and backwash balance matters.

notes.b: The balance between swash (water running up the beach) and backwash (water draining back down) decides whether a beach is built up or cut back. Waves fall into two types according to which of the two is stronger.
points: Constructive waves are low, gentle, long-wavelength (far apart) and low-frequency (few waves per minute), and they spill onto the beach.
Constructive waves are typical of calm weather; their swash is stronger than their backwash, so they carry material up the beach and build it up.
Destructive waves are high, steep, short-wavelength (close together) and high-frequency (many waves per minute), and they plunge down onto the beach.
Destructive waves are typical of storms; their backwash is stronger than their swash, so they drag material out to sea and erode the beach.
notes.tip: True/false questions test this pair: destructive means backwash stronger than swash, constructive means swash stronger than backwash. Never swap them. You may also be asked for a short explanation of constructive waves.

notes.b: Real coasts are not straight, so waves do not hit them evenly. Refraction (the bending of waves) shows why some parts of a coast erode while others receive sediment.
points: Refraction: waves approaching an indented coast slow down first in shallow water off headlands (points of land jutting into the sea), so the wave fronts bend.
Energy converges on headlands, causing more erosion there, and spreads out in bays (curved inlets of the sea), where it is weaker and deposition (the dropping of material) is favoured.
Refraction turns wave fronts until they are roughly parallel to the shore.
notes.tip: Refraction concentrates energy on headlands, not bays. Examiners also ask for a short explanation of wave refraction.

notes.b: Waves do not always strike the same part of the coast, because the level of the sea changes. Tides and storm surges change where the waves do their work.
points: Tides are the twice-daily rise and fall of sea level, caused mainly by the pull of the moon, with the sun also contributing.
Tidal range (the difference between high and low tide) sets the vertical band of coast on which the waves work, so a larger range spreads wave attack over a wider band.
A storm surge (a temporary rise in sea level during a storm) lets waves reach higher up cliffs and beaches.
Longer-term changes in land and sea level also change coasts: raised beaches (old beaches left above sea level) form emergent coasts.

Rias (drowned river valleys), fjords (flooded glacial valleys) and drowned drumlins (flooded egg-shaped hills of glacial deposit) form submergent coasts. There is more on this in the glaciation chapter, under isostasy (the rising or sinking of land).

notes.b: Waves wear away rock by four processes, and abrasion is the most effective at the foot of a cliff. Each works differently, so you need to name them and say how they work.
points: Hydraulic action: the force of breaking waves forces air and water into joints (natural cracks in rock) and cracks; the trapped air and water are compressed, then released as the wave retreats, weakening and shattering the rock.
Abrasion (corrasion): waves hurl sand, shingle and boulders against the cliff, grinding and undercutting it. It is the most effective process at the cliff base.
Attrition: rocks carried by the waves collide with each other and break into smaller, rounder pieces; attrition wears down the load (the material the waves carry) rather than the cliff.
Solution (corrosion): sea water dissolves soluble rock such as limestone.
notes.tip: If asked to name two processes of coastal erosion, give hydraulic action and abrasion, then solution and attrition. Attrition wears down the load, not the cliff, so don't present it as the main cliff-eroding process.

notes.h: Weathering, mass movement and controls on erosion
notes.b: Waves are not the only thing that wears a cliff back, and they do not erode every coast at the same speed. Processes above the waves and several controls on the rate of erosion also matter.
points: Above the waves, weathering (the breakdown of rock in place, by freeze-thaw and salt crystallisation) and mass movement (rockfalls, and slumping on soft clay cliffs) wear the cliff back.
Waves then remove the debris that falls from the cliff face, so the cliff is exposed to further attack.

Soft glacial deposits such as boulder clay (a soft mix of clay and stones left by ice) erode fastest; on the Holderness coast of Yorkshire, England, cliffs of soft boulder clay are among the fastest-eroding coastlines in Europe.
Rock structure matters: joints, faults (breaks in the rock where it has moved) and bedding (the layers in sedimentary rock) give waves lines of weakness to exploit.
Wave energy depends on fetch, storms and refraction, so a coast with a long fetch or frequent storms is eroded faster.
A beach at the foot of a cliff can absorb wave energy and protect the cliff; human activity, such as the removal of beach material, can change the rate of erosion.

notes.b: Exposure to the Atlantic or the Irish Sea decides whether a coast is eroding or depositing. The rock pattern along the coast then shapes headlands and bays.
points: The west coast faces the long Atlantic fetch and the prevailing (most common) south-westerly winds, so high-energy waves produce rugged, cliffed, erosional coasts.
The east coast faces the narrow Irish Sea, which gives a short fetch; its lower-energy waves and soft glacial deposits favour depositional features such as beaches, spits, lagoons and dunes.
Storms do most of the erosion, in short episodes; this is the temporal variation (variation over time) in coastal processes.
Where bands of hard and soft rock meet the coast at right angles (a discordant coast), the soft rock is eroded back into bays and the hard rock is left as headlands.
A concordant coast, where the rock bands run parallel to the shore, stays straighter because the outer band protects the softer rock behind it.

Headland and bay: the two landforms that result from this differential (uneven) erosion; Downpatrick Head, Co. Mayo, is a headland, and the chalk headland of Handfast Point, Dorset, England, lies between Studland Bay and Swanage Bay, which are cut into softer sands and clays.

notes.b: A cliff retreats inland as its base is undercut, leaving a platform of rock at its foot. Learn the stages in order, because exams ask you to describe how one landform of erosion forms.
points: 1. Waves erode a notch in the cliff base, between high and low tide, by hydraulic action and abrasion.
2. The rock above the notch becomes an overhang, which collapses because nothing supports it.
3. Waves remove the debris, and the cliff retreats inland, remaining steep.
4. The gently sloping rock surface left at the foot of the retreating cliff is the wave-cut platform, exposed at low tide.
5. The platform widens as the cliff retreats, until waves lose most of their energy crossing it, which slows erosion.
Example: Cliffs of Moher, Co. Clare, rise to 214 m at their highest and are made of layers of shale and sandstone.
Diagram: side view of a cliff with the notch, overhang, arrow showing retreat, and the wave-cut platform exposed at low tide.
notes.tip: The Cliffs of Moher are shale and sandstone; don't call them limestone. Photo and diagram questions ask you to pick out the cliff, wave-cut notch and wave-cut platform.

notes.h: Caves, arches, stacks and stumps (erosion sequence)
notes.b: These four features form one sequence as a headland is cut back. Each stage grows out of the one before it, so keep the order cave, arch, stack, stump.
points: 1. Waves exploit a line of weakness, a joint or fault, at the base of a headland, enlarging it by hydraulic action and abrasion to form a sea cave.
2. Caves on opposite sides of a headland meet, or one cave cuts right through, forming a sea arch.
3. The arch roof is weakened from below by wave erosion and from above by weathering, then collapses, leaving an isolated pillar called a sea stack.
4. The stack is undercut at its base and collapses into a low sea stump, which is covered at high tide.
Examples of arches: Bridges of Ross, Co. Clare, were originally three sea arches, and only one still stands; Durdle Door, Dorset, England, is a sea arch.
Examples of stacks: Dún Briste, a sea stack off Downpatrick Head, Co. Mayo; Old Harry Rocks, chalk stacks off Handfast Point, Dorset, England.
Diagram: four-stage sequence of cave, arch, stack and stump, with the joint or fault marked at the cave.
notes.tip: A stump is lower than a stack and is covered at high tide. Questions ask you to match photos of these features and to name two erosional landforms.

notes.b: A blowhole is a cave that has been enlarged upward until it opens at the cliff top. It forms where a vertical joint runs up from the cave.
points: 1. A cave is enlarged upward along a vertical joint by hydraulic action, with compressed air, until it breaks through to the cliff top, forming a blowhole.
2. In storms, spray is forced up through the hole, because the waves push water and air into the cave below.
3. If the roof between the blowhole and the sea collapses, a narrow inlet called a geo forms.
Blowholes are classified as erosional features, because the sea forms them by wearing rock away.
Diagram: vertical section of a cave connected to a vertical joint that opens at the cliff top.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to tick whether a blowhole is erosional or depositional. It is erosional.

notes.b: Waves do not only erode; they also carry material along the shore. This movement supplies the sediment that builds depositional landforms.
points: Waves carry load in the same four ways as rivers, so the river transport terms apply here too: traction (rolling along the sea bed), saltation (bouncing along it), suspension (carried within the water) and solution (dissolved in the water).
Longshore drift: waves approach the beach at an angle set by the prevailing wind; swash carries material up the beach at that angle, and backwash drags it straight back down the slope under gravity.
Repeated over time, longshore drift moves sand and shingle along the coast in a zigzag.
Longshore drift is the transport process behind spits, bars, lagoons and tombolos.
Example: on the Holderness coast, longshore drift moves eroded material southward to Spurn Head.
notes.tip: If asked to name the transport process behind spits, lagoons and tombolos, the answer is longshore drift. Groynes are a coastal defence, not a process.

notes.b: Deposition is the dropping of material that the sea has been carrying. It happens when waves lose energy and there is plenty of sediment to drop.
points: Waves deposit material when they lose energy: in constructive wave conditions, in sheltered bays, in shallow water, or after refraction has reduced their energy.
Deposition also happens where the coast changes direction, such as at a river mouth or bay.
A large supply of sediment is needed, from rivers, cliff erosion or glacial deposits offshore.
A beach is sand and shingle deposited between low tide and the highest storm waves.
Finer sand is deposited lower down the beach, and coarser shingle higher up, for example on a storm beach.
A storm beach is a ridge of large shingle thrown above normal high tide by storm waves.
Berms are ridges marking successive high-tide levels, because each tide leaves a ridge where it reached.
Examples: Tramore, Co. Waterford; Curracloe, Co. Wexford.
notes.tip: Questions on the role of deposition in forming a landform expect you to say why the waves lose energy and where the sediment comes from.

notes.b: Longshore drift keeps moving sand along the coast until the coast bends away, and there it builds a ridge. Whether the ridge is a spit or a bar depends on how far across the bay it grows.
points: 1. Longshore drift carries material past a point where the coast changes direction, such as a bay or river mouth.
2. The material is deposited in calmer, deeper water, building a ridge out from the land; a spit is attached to the land at one end only.
3. Wave refraction or a change in wind direction curves the tip, forming a recurved end.
4. Sheltered water behind the spit fills with silt, forming salt marsh or mudflat.
A sand bar (barrier beach) is a spit that grows right across the mouth of a bay, joining two headlands.

Examples: Inch and Rossbeigh, Co. Kerry, are two sand spits growing out from opposite sides of Dingle Bay; Spurn Head, at the mouth of the Humber estuary (where a river meets the sea), England, is a spit.
Diagram: plan view of a recurved spit showing the drift direction, the ridge attached to the land, the recurved tip and the salt marsh behind.
notes.tip: A spit is attached to land at one end only; a sand bar joins two headlands across a bay. Questions ask you to match photos of these and to tick sand bar as depositional.

notes.b: Two more depositional landforms follow from longshore drift: a lagoon forms when a bar cuts off part of the sea, and a tombolo forms when a ridge reaches an island.
points: A lagoon is the body of water trapped behind a sand bar; it is a depositional feature, because the bar that traps it is built from deposited sediment.
A lagoon slowly fills with sediment and vegetation because it is sheltered from the waves, and it may become marsh.
Examples: Lady's Island Lake and Tacumshin Lake, Co. Wexford, are coastal lagoons behind sand-and-gravel barriers; the Back Strand at Tramore, Co. Waterford, is another.
A tombolo is a ridge of sand or shingle joining an island to the mainland.
It is built by longshore drift and by waves refracting around the island and meeting in its shelter.
Example: Sutton, Co. Dublin, where a tombolo joins Howth Head, once an island, to the mainland.
notes.tip: A lagoon is the water behind a bar, and it is a depositional feature. A tombolo joins an island to the mainland, so don't confuse it with a spit or a bar.

notes.b: Where there is a wide, sandy beach, the wind carries dry sand inland and builds dunes. Plants, especially marram grass, are what turn loose sand into stable dunes.
points: 1. Wind blows dry sand from a wide beach at low tide inland, where it piles up against obstacles such as driftwood, seaweed and plants above high tide.
2. Marram grass colonises the sand; its long roots bind the sand, and its growth keeps pace with burial.
3. Embryo (newly forming) dunes grow into fore dunes, and further inland, as soil develops and other plants arrive, grey (fixed) dunes form.
Dune slacks are damp hollows between the dune ridges.
Damage to dunes by people is covered with the human impacts on coasts.
Examples: Brittas Bay, Co. Wicklow; Curracloe, Co. Wexford; North Bull Island, Dublin Bay.
Diagram: cross-section from beach to inland showing embryo, fore and grey dunes, and a dune slack.
notes.tip: Sand dunes are on the list of features you may be asked to match to a photo or tick as depositional.

notes.b: Every coastal landform is either erosional (made by wearing rock away) or depositional (made by dropping material). Sorting them correctly is a quick way to win marks.
points: Erosional features: cliff, wave-cut notch, wave-cut platform, cave, sea arch, sea stack, sea stump, blowhole and headland.
Depositional features: beach, storm beach, sand spit, sand bar, lagoon, tombolo, sand dunes and salt marsh.
Matching a photograph, aerial photograph or diagram to these features uses the same two classes.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to tick whether features are erosional or depositional, including blowhole, lagoon, sand bar and sand dunes. Blowhole is erosional; lagoon, sand bar and sand dunes are depositional.

notes.b: The average annual rate of coastal erosion is the total distance retreated divided by the number of years. It is a short calculation that needs the years counted correctly.
points: Step 1: subtract the earlier year from the later year to find the number of years.
Step 2: divide the total distance the cliff retreated by the number of years, so the answer is a distance per year.
Illustrative figures (invented): a cliff retreats 50 m between 1990 and 2015.
Years: 2015 minus 1990 gives 25 years.
Rate: 50 m divided by 25 years gives an average of 2 m per year.
notes.tip: Questions ask for the average annual rate of coastal erosion between two years. Find the number of years by subtracting the earlier year from the later one.

keyTerms.definition: The distance of open water over which the wind blows, which controls the size of waves.
Water rushing up the beach after a wave breaks.
Water draining back down the beach under gravity after swash.
The bending of wave fronts as they slow in shallow water off headlands, concentrating energy on headlands.
Erosion by breaking waves forcing air and water into cracks, which are compressed and then released, shattering the rock.
Erosion by sand, shingle and boulders thrown against the cliff by waves.
The breaking and rounding of rock fragments as they collide, wearing down the load.
A gently sloping rock surface left at the foot of a retreating cliff, exposed at low tide.
An isolated rock pillar left when the roof of a sea arch collapses.
A hole formed when a sea cave is enlarged upward along a joint until it breaks through to the cliff top.
The movement of sand and shingle along the coast, as swash carries material up the beach at an angle and backwash drags it straight back down.
A ridge of sand or shingle built out from the land by longshore drift and attached to it at one end.
The curved tip of a spit, formed by wave refraction or a change in wind direction.
A body of water trapped behind a sand bar, which slowly fills with sediment.
A ridge of sand or shingle joining an island to the mainland.
A dune grass whose long roots bind the sand, allowing sand dunes to form and grow.

factCards.term: Waves: three factors that control their size, and why they break
factCards.definition: Wind speed, how long the wind blows, and fetch. In shallow water, friction with the sea bed slows the base of the wave while the crest keeps moving, so the crest topples forward and the wave breaks.

factCards.term: Constructive vs destructive waves: how each affects a beach
factCards.definition: Constructive: low, long wavelength, low frequency; they spill, swash is stronger than backwash, so they build the beach up (calm weather). Destructive: high, steep, short wavelength, high frequency; they plunge, backwash is stronger, so they erode it (storms).

factCards.term: Wave refraction: what happens to wave energy at headlands and bays
factCards.definition: Waves slow first in the shallow water off headlands, so the wave fronts bend; energy converges on headlands, causing more erosion, and spreads out in bays, where it is weaker and deposition is favoured. Wave fronts end up roughly parallel to the shore.

factCards.term: Headlands and bays: how differential erosion forms them, with an example
factCards.definition: Where bands of hard and soft rock meet the coast at right angles (a discordant coast), the soft rock is eroded back into bays and the hard rock is left as headlands. Example: the chalk headland of Handfast Point, Dorset, between Studland Bay and Swanage Bay.

factCards.term: West vs east coast of Ireland: why they differ
factCards.definition: West: the long Atlantic fetch and prevailing south-westerly winds give high-energy waves and rugged, cliffed, erosional coasts. East: the narrow Irish Sea gives a short fetch and weaker waves, and soft glacial deposits favour beaches, spits, lagoons and dunes.

factCards.term: Rate of coastal erosion: five factors that control it
factCards.definition: Rock type, as soft boulder clay erodes fastest, e.g. the Holderness coast, Yorkshire; rock structure (joints, faults, bedding); wave energy (fetch, storms, refraction); whether a beach protects the cliff foot; human activity, such as removing beach material.

factCards.term: Cliffs: how weathering and mass movement help wear them back
factCards.definition: Above the waves, freeze-thaw and salt crystallisation weather the cliff face, and rockfalls and slumping on soft clay cliffs bring material down; the waves then remove the fallen debris.

factCards.term: Cliff and wave-cut platform: how they form, in stages
factCards.definition: First, waves cut a notch between high and low tide by hydraulic action and abrasion; then the overhang collapses and waves remove the debris, so the cliff retreats, staying steep; the platform left at its foot widens until waves lose energy crossing it.

factCards.term: Cliffs of Moher: their height and rock type
factCards.definition: The Cliffs of Moher, Co. Clare, rise to 214 m at their highest and are made of layers of shale and sandstone, not limestone.

factCards.term: Cave, arch, stack and stump: how the sequence forms
factCards.definition: Waves exploit a joint or fault at the base of a headland, enlarging it into a cave by hydraulic action and abrasion; caves meet through the headland as an arch; waves and weathering bring down the roof, leaving a stack; the stack is undercut to a low stump.

factCards.term: Name examples of sea arches and sea stacks
factCards.definition: Arches: the Bridges of Ross, Co. Clare (originally three, now one); Durdle Door, Dorset, England. Stacks: Dún Briste, off Downpatrick Head, Co. Mayo; Old Harry Rocks, chalk stacks off Handfast Point, Dorset.

factCards.term: Blowhole and geo: how they form
factCards.definition: Hydraulic action, with compressed air, enlarges a cave upward along a vertical joint until it breaks through to the cliff top; storm spray is forced up through the hole; if the roof between the blowhole and the sea collapses, a narrow inlet (a geo) forms.

factCards.term: Longshore drift: how it works and the landforms it builds
factCards.definition: Waves approach at an angle set by the prevailing wind; swash carries material up the beach at that angle and backwash drags it straight down, moving it along in a zigzag. It builds spits, bars, lagoons and tombolos, e.g. Spurn Head from Holderness sediment.

factCards.term: Coastal deposition: three conditions that cause it
factCards.definition: Waves lose energy (constructive waves, sheltered bays, shallow water, or after refraction); the coast changes direction, e.g. at a river mouth or bay; and there is a large supply of sediment from rivers, cliff erosion or glacial deposits offshore.

factCards.term: Beach: how its material is sorted, two features on it, and two Irish examples
factCards.definition: Finer sand lies lower down the beach and coarser shingle higher up; a storm beach is a ridge of large shingle thrown above normal high tide; berms are ridges marking successive high-tide levels. Examples: Tramore, Co. Waterford; Curracloe, Co. Wexford.

factCards.term: Sand spit: how it forms, in stages
factCards.definition: Longshore drift carries material past a point where the coast changes direction and drops it in calmer, deeper water, building a ridge attached to land at one end; refraction or a wind shift curves the tip; silt fills the sheltered water behind as salt marsh.

factCards.term: Name four sand spits, three of them Irish
factCards.definition: Inch and Rossbeigh, Co. Kerry, growing out from opposite sides of Dingle Bay; Tramore, Co. Waterford, a spit with dunes and the Back Strand lagoon behind it; Spurn Head, at the mouth of the Humber estuary, England.

factCards.term: Sand bar and lagoon: how they form, with Irish examples
factCards.definition: A spit grows right across the mouth of a bay, joining two headlands as a sand bar; the water trapped behind it is a lagoon, which slowly fills with sediment and may become marsh. Examples: Lady's Island Lake and Tacumshin Lake, Co. Wexford.

factCards.term: Tombolo: how it forms, with an Irish example
factCards.definition: Longshore drift, and waves refracting around an island and meeting in its shelter, build a ridge of sand or shingle that joins the island to the mainland. Example: Sutton, Co. Dublin, joining Howth Head, once an island.

factCards.term: Sand dunes: how they form, in stages
factCards.definition: First, wind blows dry sand from a wide beach at low tide inland, piling it against obstacles above high tide; then marram grass colonises it, its roots binding the sand; embryo dunes grow into fore dunes, and grey (fixed) dunes form inland as soil develops.

factCards.term: Name four Irish sand dune systems
factCards.definition: Brittas Bay, Co. Wicklow; Curracloe, Co. Wexford; Inch, Co. Kerry; North Bull Island, Dublin Bay.

factCards.term: Classify coastal features as erosional or depositional
factCards.definition: Erosional: cliff, wave-cut notch, wave-cut platform, cave, sea arch, sea stack, sea stump, blowhole, headland. Depositional: beach, storm beach, sand spit, sand bar, lagoon, tombolo, sand dunes, salt marsh.

factCards.term: Skill: how to work out the average annual rate of coastal erosion
factCards.definition: Subtract the earlier year from the later to get the number of years, then divide the distance retreated by it. Illustrative, invented figures: a cliff retreats 50 m between 1990 and 2015, so 50 ÷ 25 = 2 m per year.

questions.prompt: Examine the role of the process of deposition in the formation of one coastal landform that you have studied.
questions.model: Deposition occurs when waves and currents lose energy, in sheltered water or where the coast changes direction. A sand spit is built by deposition of material carried along the coast by longshore drift. The supply of sediment comes from rivers, cliff erosion or glacial deposits offshore. Longshore drift moves the material in a zigzag, as swash carries it up the beach at an angle and backwash drags it straight back down under gravity. When the drift reaches a point where the coast changes direction, such as a bay or river mouth, the material is deposited in calmer, deeper water. Deposition builds a ridge out from the land, so the spit grows outward and is attached to the land at one end only. Wave refraction or a change in wind direction curves the tip, forming a recurved end. Sheltered water behind the spit then receives fine silt, which builds up into salt marsh or mudflat. Inch, Co. Kerry, is a sand spit growing out from one side of Dingle Bay, while Rossbeigh grows from the opposite side. Diagram: a plan view showing the direction of drift along the coast, the ridge attached to the land, the recurved tip and the salt marsh behind the spit.

questions.prompt: Explain, with the aid of a labelled diagram, the formation of one landform of coastal erosion.
questions.model: A sea stack forms from a headland through a sequence of cave, arch, stack and stump. A line of weakness, such as a joint or fault, at the base of a headland is exploited by waves. Hydraulic action compresses air and water into the crack, and abrasion, from sand and boulders thrown against the rock, enlarges it into a sea cave. Caves on opposite sides of the headland enlarge until they meet or one cuts right through, forming a sea arch. Waves erode the arch from below, and weathering attacks it from above, weakening the roof. The roof collapses, leaving an isolated pillar called a sea stack. The base of the stack is undercut by waves and eventually collapses, leaving a low sea stump that is covered at high tide. Dún Briste, a sea stack off Downpatrick Head, Co. Mayo, shows this stage of the sequence. Diagram: a labelled four-stage sequence of cave, arch, stack and stump, with the joint or fault marked at the cave, and the direction of wave attack shown with arrows.

questions.prompt: Explain briefly what is meant by (a) constructive waves and (b) wave refraction.
questions.model: (a) Constructive waves are low, gentle waves with long wavelengths and low frequency. They spill onto the beach, and their swash is stronger than their backwash, so they carry material up the beach and build it up. They are typical of calm weather. (b) Wave refraction is the bending of wave fronts as they approach an indented coast. The waves slow down first in shallow water off headlands, so the wave fronts bend. Energy converges on headlands and spreads out in bays. The wave fronts end up roughly parallel to the shore.
